title: Dynamic arrays: size decided at run time

visuals.title: A dynamic array is used exactly like a normal array
int *marks = new int[3]: one pointer, three boxes on the heap

steps.note: Three int boxes in a row on the heap. marks stores the address of the first one. The values are not set yet.
The user types 80. marks[0] is the first box.
65 goes to the next box, 4 bytes further.
92 goes to the third box.
delete[] gives back ALL three boxes at once.
marks no longer points to the freed memory.

goal: After this you can create an array whose size the user types at run time, use it like a normal array, free it with delete[], and grow it by copying into a bigger array.
warmup: A canteen owner does not know how many students will come to lunch today. A fixed list of 100 plates wastes space, and 20 plates may be too few. A smart owner counts the class first, then lays out exactly that many plates. A dynamic array does the same: it waits until the program knows the size, then allocates exactly that many boxes.
definition: A normal array needs its size written in the code, for example int a[10]. A dynamic array gets its size while the program runs: int *a = new int[n]; where n can come from cin. new[] makes n boxes in a row on the heap and returns the address of the first box. You keep it in a pointer. You use a[i] exactly like a normal array. When you are finished you free the whole array with delete[] a; (the brackets are required for arrays).
howItWorks: Read the size n first. Then write int *a = new int[n];. The pointer a is a small variable on the stack. The n boxes are on the heap, side by side, so a[0] is the first, a[1] the second, and a[i] means the same as *(a + i). Fill and print the array with ordinary for loops. Always stay inside the range 0 to n-1. At the end free it with delete[] a; and set a = nullptr;. Important pair: new goes with delete, new[] goes with delete[]. Mixing them is undefined behaviour. A heap array cannot grow in place. To make it bigger: (1) allocate a new bigger array, (2) copy the old values, (3) delete[] the old array, (4) make the pointer point to the new array. A two-dimensional dynamic array is only a variation: allocate an array of pointers (int **g = new int*[rows];), then give each row its own int array with new int[cols], and free every row first, then the array of pointers.

worked.problem: Read how many marks the user has, read that many marks into a dynamic array, print their sum, and free the array.
pseudocode: FOR i = 0 to n-1: READ marks[i]
sum = 0; FOR each i: sum = sum + marks[i]
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/"Read n"/]
  B --> C["marks = new int[n]"]
  C --> D["i = 0"]
  D --> E{"i < n?"}
  E -->|Yes| F[/"Read marks[i]"/]
  F --> G["i = i + 1"]
  G --> E
  E -->|No| H["sum = 0, add all marks"]
  H --> I[/"Print sum"/]
  I --> J["delete[] marks"]
  J --> K([End])

sample.title: Size from the user, fill, sum, free

explanation.text: n will hold the size. We only learn its value when the program runs.
new int[n] creates n int boxes in a row on the heap. A normal array int a[n] needs a size known at compile time. This does not.
marks[i] works like a normal array element.
Adding all elements, the same loop as for an ordinary array.
Free the whole array with delete[] (note the brackets).
Avoid a dangling pointer.

steps.note: main starts. n has no value yet.
Ask the user for the size.
The user types 3. Now the program knows the size, but only at run time.
new int[3] takes 3 int boxes in a row from the heap. marks stores the address of the first one.
First loop, i = 0: read 80 into marks[0]. Indexing works exactly like a normal array.
i = 1: read 65.
i = 2: read 92. The loop ends when i becomes 3.
A total must start at 0.
Add marks[0]: 0 + 80.
Add marks[1]: 80 + 65.
Add marks[2]: 145 + 92.
Print the total.
delete[] gives back the WHOLE array, all 3 boxes. Brackets are required for arrays.
Make the pointer safe.

worked.problem: Read n. Make a dynamic array whose element i holds (i+1) squared. Print the elements on one line, then print the largest.
pseudocode: big = sq[0]; FOR i = 1 to n-1: IF sq[i] > big THEN big = sq[i]
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD

  B --> C["sq = new int[n]"]
  C --> D["sq[i] = (i+1)*(i+1) for each i"]
  D --> E[/"Print all elements"/]
  E --> F["big = sq[0]"]
  F --> G{"Next sq[i] > big?"}
  G -->|Yes| H["big = sq[i]"]
  H --> G
  G -->|No more| I[/"Print big"/]
  I --> J["delete[] sq"]
  J --> K([End])

sample.title: Fill by a rule, print with pointer style, find the largest

explanation.text: Five int boxes (when n is 5). Their values are not set yet.
Element i gets (i+1) squared: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
*(sq + i) means exactly the same as sq[i]. It is the pointer way to read element i.
Print a space between numbers but not after the last one.
Start with the first element as the largest so far.
Same largest-element logic as for a normal array.
One delete[] frees all n boxes.

worked.problem: An array of 3 numbers (10, 20, 30) is full. Write code that makes it twice as big without losing the numbers, adds 40, 50, 60, prints everything, and frees the memory correctly.

sample.title: Growing an array: new bigger array, copy, delete the old one

explanation.text: The array starts with room for 3 numbers.
A heap array cannot grow in place. So we make a NEW array twice as big.
Copy every old value into the new array.
The old array is no longer needed: free it.
a now points to the big array. bigger and a hold the same address.
Only a should own the array now.
Keep the size variable in step with the real size, 6.
Fill only the new slots, indexes 3, 4 and 5.
Finally free the array that a points to. There is exactly one delete[] for each new[].

variations.when: The usual form. Values are NOT set (garbage).
You want every element to start at 0.
A fixed small size with starting values.
Both read element i. Use whichever is clearer.

variations.way: Resize: new bigger array + copy + delete[] old
variations.when: The array is full and more room is needed.
A table whose rows and columns are known only at run time. Only a brief variation.

mistakes.wrong:
int *a = new int[5];
delete a;      // missing []
mistakes.error: No compiler message in most cases. new[] must be paired with delete[]. Plain delete on an array is undefined behaviour: it may leak, corrupt memory or crash.
No compiler message. All 5 boxes stay allocated until the program ends: a memory leak.

mistakes.wrong:
int *a = new int[3];
for (int i = 0; i <= 3; i++) a[i] = i;
mistakes.right:
int *a = new int[3];
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) a[i] = i;
mistakes.error: No compiler message. a[3] is outside the array (valid indexes are 0 to 2). The write damages other memory: undefined behaviour, maybe a crash later.
Standard C++ needs a compile-time size for a normal array. Some compilers accept this as an extension but others reject it, so for exams and portable code use new int[n].
No compiler message. The new array holds garbage and the old values are gone. Always copy BEFORE you delete[] the old array.

examTips: The key pair: new[] with delete[]. Write delete[] a; with brackets and say why.
A dynamic array is used exactly like a normal array: a[i], loops from 0 to n-1.
To resize: allocate bigger, copy, delete[] old, repoint. Write the four steps in this order.
Say why we use it: the size is known only at run time (the user types n).
Never run past the end: the last valid index is n-1.
romanSummary: Dynamic array ka size program chalte waqt tay hota hai: int *a = new int[n]; jahan n user se cin se aata hai.
Use bilkul normal array ki tarah karte hain: a[i], aur loop 0 se n-1 tak chalta hai.
Kaam khatam hone par delete[] a; likhna zaroori hai (brackets ke saath), phir a = nullptr;
new[] ke saath delete[] aur new ke saath delete use hota hai. Dono mix karna ghalat hai.
Array bara karna ho to naya bara array banao, purani values copy karo, purana delete[] karo aur pointer naye ki taraf kar do.

practice.prompt: Which statement frees the dynamic array int *a = new int[10];?
practice.explanation: new[] is always paired with delete[].

practice.prompt: When is the size in new int[n] decided?
practice.explanation: That is the whole point of a dynamic array: n may be typed by the user.
The loop stores 0, 2, 4, 6. a[3] is the fourth element, 6.
The array is 1 2 3 4 5. *(a + 2) is 3 and a[4] is 5, so the sum is 8.

practice.answer: delete a; must be delete[] a; because a was created with new[].
practice.hint: Look at how the memory was allocated.
practice.explanation: new int[5] needs delete[]. Plain delete is for a single new int.

practice.hint: Brackets are part of the answer.
practice.explanation: delete[] a; gives back all n boxes.

practice.prompt: Write a program that reads n, reads n integers into a dynamic array, prints the largest one, and frees the array.
practice.hint: Read n, new int[n], loop to read, loop to find the largest, delete[].
practice.explanation: Same steps as with a normal array, plus new int[n] at the start and delete[] at the end.

practice.answer: Use i < 3. a[3] does not exist; valid indexes are 0, 1, 2.
practice.hint: How many elements does the loop visit?
practice.explanation: <= 3 visits indexes 0, 1, 2, 3 which is four elements. The last write is outside the array.

quiz.prompt: What is the main advantage of a dynamic array?
options: Its size can be decided while the program runs
quiz.answer: Its size can be decided while the program runs
quiz.explanation: A normal array needs a compile-time size. A dynamic array does not.
Arrays use new[] and delete[]. Single boxes use new and delete.

quiz.prompt: p points to a dynamic array of n ints. What is the last valid index?
To grow a heap array from 3 to 6 elements you should:
options: Allocate a bigger array, copy, delete[] the old one, repoint
Call delete and keep using it
quiz.answer: Allocate a bigger array, copy, delete[] the old one, repoint
quiz.explanation: Changing n does not add memory. You need a new bigger block.

quiz.prompt: What does *(a + 2) mean when a is a dynamic int array?
options: a plus 2 added to every element
quiz.explanation: a + 2 is the address of the third element, and * reads it.
